title: Two hoses that run from the carburetor - Is the upper hose cut and zip tied? Is that's the one that brings fuel to the carburetor?

content:
## Diagnosing the "Knock" and the Disappearing Scooter

When a mechanic starts an engine to prove it runs, but that same engine refuses to fire once you walk away, the most likely culprit isn't internal damage—it's fuel starvation or a deliberate cut. In your case with the VIP Future Champion, the mechanic claimed a knock in the lower engine after installing new heads. However, since the scooter started immediately upon his touch but died shortly after you left, we have to look at the fuel delivery system first. Internal mechanical failure usually presents as an inability to start or severe misfiring that persists regardless of whether the bike has been running for seconds or hours; it rarely behaves like a "working then failing" switch.

You asked specifically about the two hoses on your carburetor. On most small 49cc scooters, including the VIP Future Champion, there are indeed two lines connected to the float bowl assembly. The **upper hose** typically connects directly to the fuel pump (often mounted near the front of the engine block or under the seat) and carries raw fuel into the carburetor's float chamber. The **lower hose**, conversely, usually exits the bottom of the float bowl and leads to a drain screw or, in some designs, recirculates back toward the tank if the pump is failing to maintain pressure. If you see an upper hose that has been cut and zip-tied off, this confirms a theory: someone physically blocked the fuel line after starting the bike for demonstration purposes. This is a common tactic used to avoid paying for further diagnostics when a customer balks at the price of additional repairs.

To verify if this is indeed a fuel starvation issue, you need to bypass the carburetor and check for fuel pressure directly at the pump outlet. Since these 49cc systems often rely on mechanical diaphragm pumps rather than electric ones, you can test by removing the air filter cover and manually squeezing the primer bulb (if equipped) or simply cranking the engine while watching the fuel line. If the upper hose is cut but the lower one remains intact, you might find that fuel is flowing out of the drain port instead of going to the carburetor.

Another possibility is a safety switch issue. Many scooters have a kickstand sensor and a side-stand kill switch. If the scooter was on its stand when the mechanic started it, or if he disabled an ignition relay, the engine might crank but not spark. However, given the description of the hose manipulation, blocking fuel flow is the most probable scenario.

If you suspect the upper line was tampered with, your next step is to trace the fuel from the tank back to the carburetor. Ensure the petcock (fuel valve) on the tank is in the "On" position and not accidentally set to "Reserve." If the line has been cut near the pump, you can temporarily splice it or use a short piece of tubing to bypass the zip tie and see if the engine fires up.

There is also the matter of the "knock" mentioned by the mechanic. While new heads should resolve compression issues, a persistent knock could indicate rod bearing failure or a piston issue that wasn't fully addressed during the rebuild. If restoring fuel flow gets you running but the knocking sound returns immediately under load, then the mechanical diagnosis holds water. At that point, you have your data: either fix the mechanical issue yourself to save money, or send it back and demand proof of repair with a test drive present.

In the world of troubleshooting 4-stroke engines, simplicity often wins over complexity. A cut fuel line is a simpler explanation than a catastrophic timing chain failure that somehow only manifests after thirty seconds of operation. Always verify physical connections before assuming expensive internal repairs are necessary. If you have access to a multimeter and oscilloscope, checking for spark at the plug while cranking can rule out ignition coil issues, but given the hose description, focus your energy on restoring fuel flow first.
